subject: Medicine
topic: Cardiac Tamponade Beck Triad Pulsus Paradoxus Emergent Pericardiocentesis
stem: A 56-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer presents to the emergency department with worsening dyspnea, fatigue, and chest heaviness for 3 days. On arrival, he is restless and sitting upright. Vital signs: blood pressure 86/60 mm Hg, heart rate 122/min, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Manual sphygmomanometry reveals that the first systolic Korotkoff sound appears at 86 mm Hg during expiration, but systolic sounds are heard continuously throughout all respiratory phases only when cuff pressure drops to 70 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals elevated jugular venous pressure extending to the angle of the jaw, muffled heart sounds, and clear lung fields bilaterally. 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low QRS voltage and electrical alternans. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Emergent bedside catheter pericardiocentesis under echocardiographic guidance
options.explanation: This patient presents with CARDIAC TAMPONADE characterized by BECK'S TRIAD (hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds), PULSUS PARADOXUS (>10 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure during normal inspiration; here, 86 - 70 = 16 mm Hg), sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and electrical alternans. Fluid accumulation within the rigid pericardial space causes equalization of intracardiac diastolic pressures, collapses right-sided heart chambers (right atrium in late diastole, right ventricle in early diastole), and drastically impairs ventricular filling and stroke volume, leading to obstructive shock. The definitive and life-saving management is IMMEDIATE PERICARDIOCENTESIS under echocardiographic or fluoroscopic guidance to evacuate pericardial fluid, relieve intrapericardial hypertension, and restore systemic cardiac output.

options.text: Administration of intravenous furosemide 40 mg bolus to reduce central venous congestion
options.explanation: Loop diuretics drastically decrease intravascular preload and ventricular filling, precipitating catastrophic cardiovascular collapse in cardiac tamponade.

options.text: Urgent synchronized electrical cardioversion to terminate sinus tachycardia
options.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is a critical compensatory mechanism to preserve cardiac output (CO = HR x SV) in the face of severely reduced stroke volume; cardioversion is ineffective and dangerous.

options.text: Immediate endotracheal intubation and initiation of positive pressure mechanical ventilation
options.explanation: Positive pressure ventilation increases intrathoracic pressure, dramatically reduces right heart venous return, and precipitates immediate cardiac arrest in cardiac tamponade.

options.text: Intravenous infusion of high-dose labetalol to lower myocardial shear stress
options.explanation: Beta-blockers abolish the sympathetic tachycardia that sustains cardiac output in tamponade, and vasodilators will worsen existing profound hypotension.

topic: Ventricular Septal Rupture Post-MI Oxygen Step-Up Emergent Surgery
stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit with acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with primary percutaneous coronary intervention to the left anterior descending artery 4 days ago. Suddenly, she develops acute respiratory distress, diaphoresis, and cold extremities. Blood pressure drops from 124/76 to 82/50 mm Hg, and heart rate is 114/min. Physical examination reveals elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasilar pulmonary crackles, and a new, harsh, holosystolic murmur heard loudest at the left lower sternal border, accompanied by a palpable thrill. Pulmonary artery catheterization reveals: right atrial pressure 14 mm Hg, pulmonary artery pressure 48/26 mm Hg, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 22 mm Hg. Blood oxygen saturation measurements show: superior vena cava 62%, right atrium 63%, right ventricle 84%, and pulmonary artery 85%. Which of the following is the definitive intervention for this complication?

options.text: Immediate intravenous thrombolysis followed by therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion
options.explanation: Thrombolysis is strictly contraindicated in post-MI mechanical wall rupture and will cause catastrophic intrapericardial or intraventricular hemorrhage.

options.text: Emergent surgical repair with intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation stabilization
options.explanation: This patient has developed an acute VENTRICULAR SEPTAL RUPTURE (VSR), a life-threatening mechanical complication of myocardial infarction occurring typically 3 to 5 days post-MI due to macrophage-mediated coagulative myocardial necrosis. It presents with sudden cardiogenic shock, pulmonary edema, and a HARSH HOLOSYSTOLIC MURMUR at the left lower sternal border with a PALPABLE THRILL. The pathognomonic diagnostic finding on right heart catheterization is an OXYGEN SATURATION STEP-UP (>5-7%) from the right atrium to the right ventricle: here, RA SvO2 is 63% and RV SvO2 jumps to 84% (+21%), demonstrating a left-to-right shunt across the ruptured ventricular septum. In contrast, acute papillary muscle rupture causes mitral regurgitation with large 'v' waves on PCWP without an RV oxygen step-up. Definitive management is EMERGENT SURGICAL (or percutaneous) VSR REPAIR; intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) placement provides vital temporary hemodynamic stabilization by reducing LV afterload and left-to-right shunting while bridging to the operating room.

options.text: Emergent percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty to reduce left atrial pressure
options.explanation: Mitral valvuloplasty is used for calcific mitral stenosis; the pathology here is a ventricular septal defect with oxygen step-up, not mitral stenosis.

options.text: Administration of high-dose intravenous phenylephrine to raise systemic vascular resistance
options.explanation: Pure alpha-agonists increase systemic vascular resistance, which increases afterload and worsens left-to-right shunting, accelerating pulmonary edema.

options.text: Conservative medical observation with intravenous milrinone for 6 weeks before elective repair
options.explanation: Delayed elective repair without emergent surgical consultation carries an in-hospital mortality rate approaching 90% due to progressive cardiogenic shock.

topic: Acute Limb Ischemia 6 Ps Immediate Anticoagulation Emergent Embolectomy
stem: A 72-year-old man with permanent atrial fibrillation on no anticoagulation presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe pain in his right leg that began 3 hours ago. He states that his right foot is numb and feels like 'ice'. Physical examination reveals that the right lower extremity is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-calf down to the toes. Sensation to light touch and pinprick is absent over the right dorsum of the foot, and he has marked weakness in right ankle dorsiflexion (strength 2/5). Femoral pulse is palpable bilaterally, but right popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are completely absent by palpation and undetectable by bedside handheld Doppler ultrasound. The left lower extremity is warm with palpable 2+ peripheral pulses throughout. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate sequence of interventions?

options.text: Elective outpatient non-invasive arterial duplex ultrasound and ankle-brachial index testing
options.explanation: Rutherford IIb threatened limb ischemia is a surgical emergency with a 4- to 6-hour window; delaying revascularization for non-urgent ultrasound will cause permanent paralysis and limb loss.

options.text: Administration of oral cilostazol 100 mg twice daily and progressive walking exercise program
options.explanation: Cilostazol and supervised exercise therapy are indicated for chronic stable intermittent claudication, not acute embolic limb ischemia with motor deficits.

options.text: Immediate intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus followed by emergent surgical catheter embolectomy
options.explanation: This patient has ACUTE LIMB ISCHEMIA (ALI) of the right lower extremity, classified as Rutherford Grade IIb (immediately threatened limb: sensory loss beyond toes, motor weakness/foot drop, inaudible arterial Doppler signals). In a patient with atrial fibrillation, the primary etiology is thromboembolism (most commonly lodging at the common femoral artery bifurcation or popliteal trifurcation). Management of acute limb ischemia requires an IMMEDIATE INTRAVENOUS UNFRACTIONATED HEPARIN BOLUS followed by continuous infusion to prevent thrombus propagation and protect microvascular runoff. Because motor deficits and complete absence of Doppler signals indicate an immediately threatened limb with an ischemic threshold of 4 to 6 hours before irreversible muscle necrosis (rhabdomyolysis and gangrene), EMERGENCY REVASCULARIZATION via surgical thromboembolectomy (Fogarty balloon catheter) or catheter-directed thrombolysis is mandatory without delaying for formal outpatient imaging.

options.text: Immediate right transfemoral amputation to prevent systemic rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia
options.explanation: Primary amputation is reserved for Rutherford Grade III (non-viable limb: complete anesthesia, profound muscle rigor, and absent venous/arterial Doppler signals); this patient's limb is viable if revascularized emergently.

options.text: Initiation of intravenous alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) infusion without surgical intervention
options.explanation: Prostaglandin vasodilators cannot recanalize an occluded macrovascular artery; mechanical or surgical revascularization is essential to salvage the limb.

topic: Acute Aortic Dissection Type B Esmolol Target Heart Rate Blood Pressure
stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, 'tearing' mid-back pain that radiates between his shoulder blades. He has a 20-year history of poorly controlled hypertension. Vital signs: blood pressure 196/112 mm Hg in the right arm and 192/108 mm Hg in the left arm, heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air. Physical examination reveals clear lungs, normal heart sounds without murmurs, and intact, symmetric peripheral pulses in all four extremities. Neurological examination is unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest and abdomen reveals an intimal flap originating immediately distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery and extending into the infrarenal aorta, without evidence of branch vessel malperfusion, aortic rupture, or hematoma extension into the ascending aorta. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medical therapy?

options.text: Immediate intravenous sodium nitroprusside monotherapy titrated to systolic pressure <120 mm Hg
options.explanation: Nitroprusside alone causes reflex sympathetic activation and severe reflex tachycardia, dramatically increasing dP/dt and triggering aortic rupture; beta-blockers must be given first.

options.text: Emergent open sternotomy and prosthetic graft replacement of the aortic arch
options.explanation: Open surgical repair is indicated for Stanford Type A dissections (involving the ascending aorta) or complicated Type B dissections (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain), not uncomplicated Type B.

options.text: Intravenous heparin bolus followed by dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and ticagrelor
options.explanation: Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are absolutely contraindicated in aortic dissection because they promote false-lumen expansion, hemothorax, and fatal rupture.

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to heart rate <60/min before administering vasodilators
options.explanation: This patient has an UNCOMPLICATED TYPE B ACUTE AORTIC DISSECTION (Stanford Type B / DeBakey Type III), defined as dissection originating distal to the left subclavian artery without involvement of the ascending aorta. Uncomplicated Type B dissections are primarily managed with MEDICAL THERAPY in the intensive care unit. The cornerstone of initial medical management is anti-impulse therapy to minimize aortic wall sheer stress (dP/dt). The initial drug of choice is an INTRAVENOUS SHORT-ACTING BETA-BLOCKER (e.g., ESMOLOL or labetalol) titrated to a target HEART RATE <60 BEATS/MIN. Crucially, beta-blockade must ALWAYS precede or accompany vasodilator therapy (e.g., nitroprusside or nicardipine) to prevent REFLEX TACHYCARDIA, which would drastically increase dP/dt and accelerate dissection progression or rupture. The goal is to achieve systolic blood pressure between 100 and 120 mm Hg (or lowest tolerated mean arterial pressure) and HR <60 within 20 minutes.

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine bolus administered every 2 hours to achieve diastolic pressure <80 mm Hg
options.explanation: Hydralazine causes unpredictable hypotension and marked reflex tachycardia, exacerbating aortic wall shear stress; it is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection.

topic: Cardiogenic Syncope Aortic Stenosis Structural Heart Disease Workup
stem: A 76-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his daughter after an episode of sudden loss of consciousness earlier today. He was walking up a flight of stairs carrying groceries when he suddenly felt lightheaded and collapsed without warning. He regained consciousness within 30 seconds without post-ictal confusion or tongue biting. He reports progressive exertional dyspnea and chest tightness over the past 4 months. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Physical examination reveals blood pressure 118/84 mm Hg, heart rate 68/min, and regular rhythm. Carotid upstrokes are markedly delayed and diminished in amplitude (pulsus parvus et tardus). Cardiovascular examination demonstrates a sustained, apical left ventricular heave and a harsh, late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur heard loudest at the right second intercostal space, radiating to both carotid arteries. S2 is soft and single. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic study?

options.text: Head-up tilt table testing to evaluate for neurocardiogenic vasovagal syncope
options.explanation: Tilt table testing is reserved for suspected vasovagal syncope without structural heart disease; it is contraindicated and unhelpful in clear valvular heart disease.

options.text: 24-hour ambulatory Holter electrocardiographic monitoring for sick sinus syndrome
options.explanation: While arrhythmia can cause syncope, this patient has overt physical signs of severe aortic stenosis on exertion; echocardiography is the primary and urgent test.

options.text: Electroencephalography and non-contrast head CT to rule out complex partial seizures
options.explanation: Rapid recovery without post-ictal state, tongue biting, or incontinence makes seizure unlikely; exertional syncope with a systolic murmur is cardiogenic.

options.text: Subcutaneous implantable loop recorder placement prior to cardiac imaging
options.explanation: Implantable loop recorders are used for unexplained recurrent syncope after negative echocardiographic and rhythm evaluations, not when exam shows severe AS.

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography to assess aortic valve area and transvalvular gradient
options.explanation: This patient experienced CARDIOGENIC (EXERTIONAL) SYNCOPE secondary to SEVERE AORTIC STENOSIS (AS). The classic triad of symptomatic aortic stenosis consists of ANGINA, SYNCOPE (exertional), and DYSPNEA (heart failure). Physical examination demonstrates classic features: (1) PULSUS PARVUS ET TARDUS (slow-rising, low-amplitude carotid pulse); (2) Late-peaking harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to carotids; (3) Soft or absent A2 with single S2 (due to calcified immobile leaflets); and (4) Sustained apical heave. Syncope during exertion occurs because the fixed stenotic valve orifice cannot increase cardiac output to meet the exercise-induced skeletal muscle vasodilation, resulting in severe systemic hypotension and cerebral hypoperfusion, or exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmias. The definitive initial diagnostic test is TRANSTHORACIC ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY (TTE) to evaluate aortic valve area (<1.0 cm2 = severe), peak velocity (>4.0 m/s), and mean transvalvular gradient (>40 mm Hg). The onset of syncope indicates critical AS and is a class I indication for urgent aortic valve replacement (SAVR or TAVR).

subject: Medicine
topic: Hypertensive Emergency Clevidipine Target Blood Pressure Reduction Threshold
stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe throbbing headache, blurred vision, and nausea for 6 hours. He ran out of his antihypertensive medications 3 weeks ago. On examination, he is alert but distressed. Vital signs: blood pressure 228/134 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral optic disc edema (papilledema), flame hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots. Neurological examination reveals no focal motor or sensory deficits. Serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL 6 months ago), and urinalysis shows 2+ proteinuria with microscopic hematuria. Head CT shows no acute intracranial hemorrhage. Which of the following represents the most appropriate blood pressure management strategy over the first hour of treatment?

options.text: Initiation of intravenous clevidipine or nicardipine to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 20% to 25%
options.explanation: This patient has a HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCY (formerly malignant hypertension), defined as severe blood pressure elevation (typically systolic >180 and/or diastolic >120 mm Hg) associated with ACUTE TARGET-ORGAN DAMAGE: here, grade IV hypertensive retinopathy (papilledema, hemorrhages), acute kidney injury, and hypertensive encephalopathy. In hypertensive emergencies (except acute aortic dissection, acute ischemic stroke, or pheochromocytoma), blood pressure must be lowered gradually using INTRAVENOUS ANTIHYPERTENSIVES (e.g., CLEVIDIPINE, NICARDIPINE, or labetalol). The gold-standard guideline recommendation is to REDUCE MEAN ARTERIAL PRESSURE (MAP) BY NO MORE THAN 20% TO 25% WITHIN THE FIRST HOUR. If stable, blood pressure is lowered toward 160/100-110 mm Hg over the next 2 to 6 hours, and gradually normalized over 24 to 48 hours. Excessive or precipitous blood pressure reduction shifts cerebral and renal autoregulation curves, precipitating cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemic stroke, and acute tubular necrosis.

options.text: Immediate aggressive reduction of blood pressure to <120/80 mm Hg within 30 minutes
options.explanation: Precipitous normalization of BP abolishes autoregulatory cerebral and renal perfusion, causing catastrophic watershed ischemic stroke and acute renal failure.

options.text: Oral administration of sublingual nifedipine capsules every 30 minutes until diastolic pressure is <90 mm Hg
options.explanation: Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrollable, rapid drops in blood pressure with severe reflex tachycardia, and has been associated with myocardial infarction and stroke; it is contraindicated.

options.text: Intravenous bolus of hydralazine 20 mg repeated every 15 minutes to target systolic pressure <140 mm Hg
options.explanation: Hydralazine has a delayed, prolonged, and unpredictable hypotensive response with profound reflex tachycardia, making it unsuitable for titratable emergency management.

options.text: Intravenous sodium nitroprusside titrated aggressively without continuous arterial line pressure monitoring
options.explanation: Nitroprusside requires continuous arterial line monitoring to prevent profound hypotension and cyanide toxicity, and clevidipine/nicardipine are safer first-line choices.

subject: Medicine
topic: Infective Endocarditis Severe Aortic Regurgitation Urgent Valve Surgery
stem: A 42-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents with persistent fevers, chills, and progressive shortness of breath for 5 days. Vital signs: temperature 38.9 C (102 F), blood pressure 102/44 mm Hg, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on 4 L nasal cannula. Physical examination reveals elevated JVP, bilateral diffuse pulmonary crackles, a wide pulse pressure (58 mm Hg), and a soft, early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left third intercostal space. Petechiae are noted on the conjunctivae, and splinter hemorrhages are visible beneath several fingernails. Blood cultures from three separate venipuncture sites grow methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Transthoracic echocardiogram reveals a 14-mm mobile vegetation on the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve with flail leaflet and severe, acute aortic regurgitation causing premature closure of the mitral valve. Intravenous cefazolin is initiated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Completion of a full 6-week course of intravenous cefazolin before surgical consideration
options.explanation: Delaying surgery to complete antibiotics in severe acute aortic regurgitation with pulmonary edema leads to irreversible cardiogenic shock and death.

options.text: Urgent aortic valve replacement surgery during the current hospital admission
options.explanation: This patient has NATIVE VALVE INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS (IE) caused by Staphylococcus aureus complicated by SEVERE ACUTE AORTIC REGURGITATION and ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE (pulmonary edema, wide pulse pressure, premature mitral valve closure due to marked elevated LV end-diastolic pressure). Although intravenous bactericidal antibiotics (cefazolin for MSSA) must be started immediately, MEDICAL THERAPY ALONE IS INSUFFICIENT AND ASSOCIATED WITH EXTREME MORTALITY. The 2023 ESC and ACC/AHA guidelines establish definitive indications for URGENT/EMERGENT SURGICAL VALVE INTERVENTION in IE: (1) Heart failure directly caused by severe acute regurgitation or valve obstruction (the strongest indication); (2) Uncontrolled infection (persistent bacteremia >5-7 days despite appropriate antibiotics, perivalvular abscess, fistula, or large fungal/MDR organism); and (3) Prevention of systemic embolism in patients with persistent vegetations >10 mm, especially after an embolic event or with mobile vegetations >15 mm. Surgery should not be delayed to 'complete a course of antibiotics' in the presence of refractory cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

options.text: Addition of oral rifampin and intravenous gentamicin to medical therapy without surgical consult
options.explanation: Rifampin is indicated only for PROSTHETIC valve staphylococcal endocarditis (to penetrate biofilm); adding it to native valve endocarditis provides no benefit and causes resistance and toxicity.

options.text: Placement of a temporary intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation pump for hemodynamic support
options.explanation: Intra-aortic balloon pump counterpulsation is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in aortic regurgitation because balloon inflation during diastole markedly worsens retrograde regurgitant flow into the LV.

topic: Low-Flow Low-Gradient Aortic Stenosis Dobutamine Stress Echocardiography
stem: A 74-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and prior coronary artery bypass grafting presents with worsening exertional dyspnea (NYHA Class III) over the past 6 months. Physical examination reveals blood pressure 110/72 mm Hg, heart rate 72/min, elevated JVP of 8 cm H2O, and a soft, mid-systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border with a single second heart sound. Resting transthoracic echocardiogram reveals left ventricular ejection fraction of 28%, stroke volume index of 28 mL/m2 (reference >35 mL/m2), calculated aortic valve area (AVA) of 0.8 cm2 (reference <1.0 cm2 for severe), mean transvalvular gradient of 28 mm Hg (reference >40 mm Hg for severe), and peak transaortic jet velocity of 3.2 m/s. Which of the following diagnostic tests is most appropriate to distinguish true severe aortic stenosis from pseudo-severe aortic stenosis in this patient?

options.text: Cardiopulmonary exercise stress testing with treadmill ramp protocol to maximum exhaustion
options.explanation: Exercise treadmill testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis and can precipitate acute syncope or fatal ventricular arrhythmia.

options.text: Coronary CT angiography to evaluate patency of existing saphenous vein bypass grafts
options.explanation: Coronary graft imaging assesses ischemia, but does not resolve whether the low transvalvular gradient represents true severe vs pseudo-severe valvular stenosis.

options.text: Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography to assess contractile reserve and valve area changes
options.explanation: This patient has CLASSICAL LOW-FLOW, LOW-GRADIENT AORTIC STENOSIS (LFLG-AS) WITH REDUCED EJECTION FRACTION, defined by: (1) Calculated aortic valve area <= 1.0 cm2; (2) Mean gradient <40 mm Hg (or peak velocity <4.0 m/s); (3) LVEF <50%; and (4) Stroke volume index <= 35 mL/m2. In this setting, the low cardiac output cannot generate sufficient transvalvular flow to produce a high pressure gradient, creating a clinical dilemma between: (A) TRUE SEVERE AS: where the valve is severely calcified and rigid, and (B) PSEUDO-SEVERE AS: where the primary problem is severe myocardial dysfunction that cannot generate sufficient forward force to fully open an only moderately stenotic valve. The recommended diagnostic investigation is LOW-DOSE DOBUTAMINE STRESS ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY (DSE, infusing dobutamine from 2.5 up to 20 ug/kg/min). DSE evaluates two critical parameters: (1) CONTRACTILE RESERVE (defined as an increase in stroke volume by >= 20%); and (2) VALVE KINETICS under flow. In true severe AS, as stroke volume increases, the AVA remains fixed (<= 1.0 cm2) while mean gradient rises to >= 40 mm Hg. In pseudo-severe AS, the valve opening improves (AVA increases to >1.0 cm2) with minimal change in gradient. Patients with true severe AS and contractile reserve benefit dramatically from transcatheter or surgical aortic valve replacement.

options.text: Right heart catheterization with pulmonary vasodilator challenge using inhaled nitric oxide
options.explanation: Nitric oxide challenge evaluates reversibility of pulmonary arterial hypertension in pre-transplant workups, not the hemodynamic severity of aortic stenosis.

options.text: Measurement of serum cardiac troponin I and B-type natriuretic peptide every 8 hours
options.explanation: Biomarkers reflect myocardial wall stress, but cannot differentiate true-severe from pseudo-severe mechanical valve narrowing.

subject: Medicine
topic: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Outflow Tract Obstruction Beta-Blocker Avoid CCB
stem: A 22-year-old collegiate basketball player undergoes medical evaluation for recurrent episodes of lightheadedness and chest tightness occurring during high-intensity wind sprints. His paternal uncle died suddenly at age 26 while playing soccer. Physical examination reveals a dynamic, harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard loudest at the left sternal border without carotid radiation. The murmur increases significantly in intensity when the patient moves from a squatting to a standing position and during the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver; it decreases in intensity during passive leg elevation. 12-lead ECG demonstrates marked left ventricular hypertrophy with deep, narrow 'dagger-like' Q waves in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6). Transthoracic echocardiogram reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy with an interventricular septal thickness of 22 mm (reference <12 mm), systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve with dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction (peak resting gradient 48 mm Hg), and LVEF 72%. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for this patient?

options.text: Oral amlodipine 10 mg daily to reduce systemic vascular resistance and afterload
options.explanation: Dihydropyridine CCBs cause peripheral vasodilation, decreasing LV preload and chamber size, which drastically increases dynamic LVOT obstruction and can trigger fatal syncope.

options.text: Sublingual nitroglycerin tablets taken 5 minutes prior to basketball practice
options.explanation: Nitrates decrease venous preload, reducing LV cavity volume and severely worsening outflow tract obstruction; they are absolutely contraindicated in obstructive HCM.

options.text: Oral digoxin 0.25 mg daily to enhance left ventricular inotropic ejection performance
options.explanation: Digoxin increases myocardial contractility, which intensifies systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet and worsens the outflow gradient; inotropic agents are contraindicated.

options.text: Oral metoprolol succinate or nadolol titrated to resting heart rate 55 to 60 beats/min
options.explanation: This patient has HYPERTROPHIC CARDIOMYOPATHY (HCM) WITH DYNAMIC LVOT OBSTRUCTION. The dynamic murmur of HCM is uniquely characterized by its behavior with preload/afterload maneuvers: MANEUVERS THAT DECREASE LV CAVITY SIZE (standing, Valsalva strain, dehydration, vasodilators) INCREASE LVOT OBSTRUCTION and MAKE THE MURMUR LOUDER; conversely, maneuvers that increase cavity volume (squatting, passive leg raise, handgrip) decrease the gradient and soften the murmur. The primary pathophysiological driver of obstruction is systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve leaflet contacting the hypertrophied septum. FIRST-LINE MEDICAL PHARMACOTHERAPY consists of NON-VASODILATING BETA-BLOCKERS (e.g., METOPROLOL, NADOLOL, or propranolol) or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil). Beta-blockers exert negative inotropic effects (reducing ejection velocity and dynamic suction on the mitral leaflet) and negative chronotropic effects (prolonging diastolic filling time, thereby increasing end-diastolic LV cavity size and widening the outflow tract). In contrast, DIHYDROPYRIDINE CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS (e.g., AMLODIPINE, NIFEDIPINE), NITRATES, ACE INHIBITORS, AND DIURETICS ARE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED because peripheral vasodilation or volume depletion collapses LV cavity dimensions, dramatically worsening LVOT obstruction and precipitating syncope or cardiovascular collapse.

options.text: Immediate referral for permanent surgical ventricular septal myectomy without trial of medication
options.explanation: Surgical septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation is indicated for patients with refractory NYHA class III/IV symptoms despite optimal medical therapy, not as first-line initial treatment.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure Nitroprusside in Severe Mitral Regurgitation
stem: A 64-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit with acute decompensated heart failure and flash pulmonary edema. She has a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy with severe functional mitral regurgitation. On arrival, she is sitting upright in extreme respiratory distress with diffuse bibasilar crackles and wheezing throughout both lung fields. Vital signs: blood pressure 184/108 mm Hg, heart rate 106/min, respiratory rate 32/min, oxygen saturation 86% on 100% non-rebreather mask. Bedside echocardiogram reveals LVEF 30% and severe central mitral regurgitation with a large jet filling the left atrium. Despite intravenous boluses of furosemide (total 120 mg) and initiation of bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP), her systolic blood pressure remains 178 mm Hg, and she has persistent severe dyspnea with worsening hypercapnia. Arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.28, PaCO2 52 mm Hg, PaO2 64 mm Hg. Which of the following intravenous medications is most appropriate to initiate immediately to reduce left ventricular afterload and regurgitant volume?

options.text: Continuous intravenous norepinephrine infusion to maintain coronary perfusion pressure
options.explanation: Norepinephrine is a potent alpha-1 agonist that increases systemic vascular resistance, which would drastically worsen afterload, regurgitant fraction, and pulmonary edema.

options.text: Intravenous bolus of metoprolol tartrate 5 mg to reduce myocardial oxygen demand
options.explanation: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema and severe respiratory distress due to acute negative inotropy.

options.text: Continuous intravenous vasopressin infusion to prevent splanchnic vasodilation
options.explanation: Vasopressin causes severe peripheral arterial vasoconstriction via V1 receptors, exacerbating left ventricular afterload and worsening mitral regurgitation.

options.text: High-dose intravenous epinephrine infusion to stimulate beta-1 myocardial contractility
options.explanation: Epinephrine markedly increases myocardial oxygen demand, causes ventricular arrhythmias, and raises afterload at higher doses, worsening decompensated heart failure.

options.text: Continuous intravenous sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to blood pressure
options.explanation: This patient presents with HYPERTENSIVE ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE complicated by SEVERE ACUTE FUNCTIONAL MITRAL REGURGITATION and FLASH PULMONARY EDEMA. In functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation, severe systemic hypertension markedly increases LEFT VENTRICULAR AFTERLOAD. Elevated afterload impedes forward aortic ejection and preferentially drives regurgitant blood flow backwards across the incompetent mitral valve into the left atrium and pulmonary venous circulation, triggering catastrophic pulmonary capillary hydrostatic transudation and alveolar flooding. When high-dose loop diuretics and non-invasive ventilation fail to control severe hypertension and flash pulmonary edema, the treatment of choice is IMMEDIATE INTRAVENOUS AFTERLOAD REDUCTION using SODIUM NITROPRUSSIDE. Nitroprusside is a potent balanced arterial and venous vasodilator that directly generates nitric oxide in vascular smooth muscle. By lowering systemic vascular resistance (arterial afterload reduction), it facilitates forward left ventricular stroke volume into the aorta, dramatically decreases retrograde regurgitant volume across the mitral valve, and reduces pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, reversing life-threatening pulmonary edema.

subject: Medicine
topic: Atrial Fibrillation with WPW Procainamide vs AV Nodal Blockade Contraindication
stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset rapid palpitations, dizziness, and shortness of breath that began 45 minutes ago. He has no chronic medical conditions. Vital signs: blood pressure 114/74 mm Hg, heart rate 190/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiovascular examination reveals an irregularly irregular tachycardia without murmurs. 12-lead ECG demonstrates an irregularly irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes of varying morphologies, rapid ventricular rates fluctuating between 180 and 240 beats/min, and a bizarre, polymorphic appearance without organized P waves. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous pharmacotherapy to administer?

options.text: Intravenous procainamide or ibutilide to prolong refractory periods
options.explanation: This patient presents with ATRIAL FIBRILLATION WITH PRE-EXCITATION (WOLFF-PARKINSON-WHITE [WPW] SYNDROME). The pathognomonic ECG signature of pre-excited AF is: (1) Irregularly irregular rhythm (AF); (2) Wide, bizarre QRS complexes resulting from anomalous antegrade conduction down the accessory pathway (bundle of Kent); (3) Beat-to-beat variability in QRS width and morphology (representing fluctuating degrees of fusion between accessory and AV nodal conduction); and (4) Extremely rapid ventricular rates (>200-250 beats/min, because the accessory pathway has a shorter refractory period than the AV node). In hemodynamically stable patients, the pharmacotherapy of choice is INTRAVENOUS PROCAINAMIDE (or ibutilide). Procainamide is a Class Ia antiarrhythmic that selectively blocks fast sodium channels and prolongs the refractory period of the accessory pathway and atrial myocardium, slowing ventricular conduction and converting AF to sinus rhythm. Crucially, AV NODAL BLOCKING AGENTS (adenosine, beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers [diltiazem, verapamil], and digoxin) ARE ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED. Blocking the AV node preferentially shunts 100% of chaotic fibrillatory impulses (up to 300-600/min) down the accessory pathway, precipitating rapid degeneration into VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION and sudden cardiac arrest. If the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain), immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion is mandatory.

options.text: Intravenous diltiazem bolus followed by continuous infusion for rate control
options.explanation: Diltiazem blocks the AV node, directing rapid fibrillatory atrial conduction exclusively down the accessory pathway and triggering fatal ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Intravenous metoprolol tartrate bolus administered over 2 minutes
options.explanation: Beta-blockers block the AV node and are strictly contraindicated in pre-excited AF because they accelerate antegrade conduction through the accessory pathway.

options.text: Rapid intravenous bolus of adenosine 6 mg via antecubital vein
options.explanation: Adenosine causes transient complete AV nodal block; in pre-excited AF, this causes preferential accessory conduction and precipitates ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Intravenous digoxin bolus to enhance parasympathetic AV conduction delay
options.explanation: Digoxin blocks the AV node and actually shortens the refractory period of the accessory pathway, dramatically increasing the risk of lethal ventricular fibrillation.

topic: Sustained Monomorphic Ventricular Tachycardia Hemodynamically Stable Therapy
stem: A 63-year-old man with a history of anterior myocardial infarction 3 years ago and ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 32%) presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset, steady heart fluttering and mild lightheadedness for 2 hours. He denies chest pain, syncope, or shortness of breath. Vital signs: blood pressure 118/76 mm Hg, heart rate 158/min, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Cardiovascular examination reveals regular tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no peripheral edema. 12-lead ECG demonstrates a regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia with a QRS duration of 160 ms, left bundle branch block morphology, extreme northwest axis (-120 degrees), and clear atrioventricular dissociation with occasional capture and fusion beats. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Immediate unsynchronized high-energy defibrillation at 200 J biphasic
options.explanation: Defibrillation is unsynchronized and reserved for pulseless cardiac arrest (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless VT); delivering an unsynchronized shock during the T wave of a stable VT can induce ventricular fibrillation (R-on-T phenomenon).

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone infusion 150 mg over 10 minutes
options.explanation: This patient has SUSTAINED MONOMORPHIC VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA (VT), confirmed by the presence of: (1) Wide-complex regular tachycardia (>120 ms); (2) Atrioventricular (AV) dissociation; (3) Capture and fusion beats (pathognomonic of VT); (4) Extreme axis deviation; and (5) Prior structural heart disease (prior myocardial infarction with scar-related re-entrant circuit). Although wide-complex tachycardia in a patient with prior MI should ALWAYS be presumed to be VT until proven otherwise, this patient is currently HEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE (normal blood pressure 118/76, alert, no ischemic chest pain, no pulmonary edema). In hemodynamically stable monomorphic VT, initial management is INTRAVENOUS ANTIARRHYTHMIC PHARMACOTHERAPY using AMIODARONE (150 mg IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1 mg/min maintenance) or PROCAINAMIDE (20-50 mg/min). If pharmacotherapy fails, or if the patient at any point develops hemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, pulmonary edema), IMMEDIATE SYNCHRONIZED DIRECT-CURRENT CARDIOVERSION (initial energy 100 J) is indicated.

options.text: Intravenous diltiazem 20 mg bolus to terminate re-entrant AV nodal conduction
options.explanation: Diltiazem is indicated for SVT, but in VT it produces catastrophic peripheral vasodilation, negative inotropy, and sudden cardiovascular collapse; CCBs are contraindicated in wide-complex tachycardia of unknown etiology.

options.text: Carotid sinus massage followed by intravenous adenosine 12 mg push
options.explanation: Vagal maneuvers and adenosine are used for supraventricular tachycardias; adenosine in ventricular tachycardia can cause severe hypotension or accelerate ventricular rates.

options.text: Emergent bedside catheter pericardiocentesis under ultrasound guidance
options.explanation: Pericardiocentesis treats cardiac tamponade, not hemodynamically stable re-entrant ventricular tachycardia.

subject: Medicine
topic: Constrictive Pericarditis Square Root Sign Dip and Plateau Pericardiectomy
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive abdominal distension, lower extremity edema, and exertional fatigue for 8 months. Two years ago, he underwent mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma, currently in complete remission. Physical examination reveals blood pressure 112/74 mm Hg, heart rate 78/min. Jugular venous distension is present up to the angle of the mandible; on inspiration, the jugular venous column rises paradoxically by 3 cm (Kussmaul sign). Cardiovascular examination demonstrates distant heart sounds and an early, high-pitched diastolic sound heard best at the left sternal border 60 ms after S2. Abdominal examination reveals marked non-tender ascites with a fluid wave and firm hepatomegaly; 3+ pitting edema is present bilaterally to the knees. Echocardiogram reveals biatrial enlargement with normal left ventricular cavity size and LVEF 58%, accompanied by pronounced respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity (>25%) and a prominent early diastolic dip and plateau ('square-root sign') on invasive ventricular pressure tracing. Which of the following is the definitive curative treatment for this condition?

options.text: Lifelong high-dose oral colchicine and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy
options.explanation: Colchicine and NSAIDs treat acute or recurrent inflammatory pericarditis, but cannot reverse end-stage dense fibrocalcific pericardial scarring in chronic constrictive pericarditis.

options.text: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) placement for cirrhotic ascites
options.explanation: The ascites is secondary to elevated central venous pressure from pericardial constriction ('cardiac cirrhosis'), not primary portal hypertension; TIPS will increase venous return and worsen heart failure.

options.text: Surgical total pericardiectomy ('pericardial stripping')
options.explanation: This patient presents with CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS, a late complication of mediastinal radiation therapy (or prior cardiac surgery, tuberculosis, or idiopathic viral pericarditis). Fibrocalcific thickening and scarring of the rigid pericardium encase the heart, preventing physiological diastolic filling. Characteristic clinical features include: (1) Severe right-sided heart failure symptoms out of proportion to left-sided symptoms (massive ascites, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, clear lung fields); (2) KUSSMAUL SIGN: paradoxical rise or failure of JVP to fall during inspiration due to impaired right ventricular compliance; (3) PERICARDIAL KNOCK: an early, high-pitched diastolic sound corresponding to the abrupt cessation of rapid ventricular filling against the rigid pericardium; (4) Prominent jugular 'y' descent; and (5) Catheterization showing ventricular interdependence and the classic 'DIP AND PLATEAU' ('SQUARE-ROOT') SIGN on diastolic ventricular pressure tracings. stem: A 34-year-old man of Southeast Asian descent is brought to the emergency department after an episode of sudden nocturnal syncope. His wife awoke to loud gasping and gurgling sounds, finding him unresponsive and twitching for approximately 1 minute before spontaneously recovering consciousness. He reports no prior medical conditions, palpitations, or exertional chest pain. His paternal uncle died suddenly in his sleep at age 32. Physical examination and bedside echocardiogram reveal a structurally normal heart with LVEF 65%. 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus rhythm at 68/min with pseudo-right bundle branch block and >2 mm coved ST-segment elevation with an inverted T wave in leads V1 and V2. Serum electrolytes, cardiac troponin I, and toxicology screen are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management to prevent sudden cardiac death in this patient?

options.text: Initiation of oral flecainide 100 mg twice daily for antiarrhythmic suppression

options.text: Elective catheter radiofrequency ablation of the atrioventricular junction
options.explanation: AV node ablation does not prevent epicardial right ventricular outflow tract polymorphic VT and would necessitate lifelong ventricular pacing.

options.explanation: Brugada arrhythmias characteristically occur at rest or during sleep (vagal predominance) or fever, not during exercise; reassurance leaves the patient at extreme risk of sudden death.

Pharmacotherapy (quinidine) can be used as an adjunct for recurrent ICD shocks, but cannot replace an ICD for definitive protection.

topic: Subclavian Steal Syndrome Retrograde Vertebral Flow Arm Claudication Workup
stem: A 64-year-old man presents with episodic lightheadedness, vertigo, and blurred vision that occur specifically when he engages in vigorous physical work with his left arm, such as painting ceilings or sawing wood. He also notes dull aching and cramping in his left arm during these activities that resolves with rest. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 40-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination reveals: blood pressure 144/82 mm Hg in the right arm and 108/70 mm Hg in the left arm (difference of 36 mm Hg). The left radial pulse is noticeably delayed and diminished compared to the right radial pulse. A systolic bruit is audible in the left supraclavicular fossa. Fundoscopic and cranial nerve examinations are normal at rest. Which of the following vascular pathophysiological mechanisms is responsible for this patient's neurological symptoms?

options.text: Microembolization of atheromatous debris from the carotid bifurcation into the middle cerebral artery
options.explanation: Carotid atheroembolism produces anterior circulation deficits (amaurosis fugax, contralateral hemiparesis, aphasia), not arm exercise-induced posterior vertebrobasilar symptoms.

options.text: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the internal carotid artery leading to intermittent dissection
options.explanation: Fibromuscular dysplasia typically affects young females and causes internal carotid narrowing without arm blood pressure discrepancies.

options.text: External compression of the vertebral artery by an aberrant cervical rib within the scalene triangle
options.explanation: Thoracic outlet syndrome compresses the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels, but does not cause retrograde vertebral flow or vertebrobasilar steal.

options.text: Incomplete development of the circle of Willis anterior communicating artery
options.explanation: Anatomical variants of the circle of Willis are common, but do not produce exertional arm claudication with blood pressure disparities.

options.text: Atherosclerotic occlusion of the proximal subclavian artery with retrograde blood flow down the ipsilateral vertebral artery
options.explanation: This patient has SUBCLAVIAN STEAL SYNDROME, caused by severe stenosis or occlusion of the PROXIMAL SUBCLAVIAN ARTERY (proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery), almost always due to atherosclerosis and most commonly involving the LEFT subclavian artery. Under resting conditions, collateral circulation may suffice. However, during vigorous physical exertion of the ipsilateral upper extremity, skeletal muscle metabolic demand triggers robust local arteriolar vasodilation, causing a precipitous drop in vascular resistance in the arm. Distal subclavian perfusion pressure falls BELOW the pressure in the vertebrobasilar arterial system. Blood is consequently 'STOLEN' from the cerebral circulation: blood flows up the contralateral vertebral artery, crosses the basilar junction, and flows IN A RETROGRADE DIRECTION DOWN THE IPSILATERAL VERTEBRAL ARTERY to supply the exercising arm. This cerebral steal produces transient vertebrobasilar insufficiency: vertigo, dizziness, ataxia, diplopia, and syncope. Diagnostic features include a systolic blood pressure disparity >15-20 mm Hg between the arms, supraclavicular bruit, and reversed flow on Doppler ultrasound. Definitive management involves endovascular stenting or surgical bypass.

topic: Right Ventricular Infarction Preload Dependence IV Fluids Avoid Nitrates
stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe crushing substernal chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea for 2 hours. 12-lead ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL, consistent with an acute inferior STEMI. Shortly after arrival, the emergency physician administers sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg. Within 3 minutes, the patient becomes profoundly lethargic and lightheaded. Vital signs: blood pressure plummets from 138/82 to 74/42 mm Hg, heart rate is 108/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination reveals flat neck veins while supine that engorge with inspiration, completely clear lung fields on auscultation, and cool, clammy extremities. Repeat right-sided 12-lead ECG reveals 1.5-mm ST-segment elevation in lead V4R. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate therapy to restore hemodynamic stability?

options.text: Rapid intravenous bolus of 1,000 mL of 0.9% normal saline to restore right ventricular preload
options.explanation: This patient has an acute INFERIOR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION COMPLICATED BY RIGHT VENTRICULAR INFARCTION (RVI), occurring in up to 30-50% of inferior STEMIs due to proximal occlusion of the RIGHT CORONARY ARTERY (RCA). RVI presents with the classic triad of: (1) HYPOTENSION, (2) ELEVATED JUGULAR VENOUS PRESSURE (or Kussmaul sign), and (3) COMPLETELY CLEAR LUNG FIELDS (in contrast to left ventricular failure, which produces pulmonary crackles). ST elevation >= 1 mm in right-sided lead V4R is highly sensitive and specific. The infarcted, non-contractile right ventricle behaves as a passive conduit and is EXQUISITELY PRELOAD-DEPENDENT: high right atrial filling pressure is required to push blood through the pulmonary circulation into the left heart. Administration of VENODILATORS (such as NITROGLYCERIN, morphine, or diuretics) drastically reduces venous return (preload), precipitating catastrophic hypotension and cardiogenic shock. The immediate treatment of choice is AGGRESSIVE INTRAVENOUS CRYSTALLOID RESUSCITATION (normal saline boluses) to restore RV filling pressure and forward cardiac output. Vasodilators and diuretics are strictly contraindicated. If shock persists after volume loading, inotropic support with dobutamine is initiated, and emergent reperfusion (primary PCI) is definitive.

options.text: Immediate intravenous infusion of furosemide 80 mg to reduce central venous pressure
options.explanation: Loop diuretics decrease preload, which is essential to maintain right ventricular filling; diuresis in RVI causes fatal circulatory collapse.

options.text: Intravenous infusion of sodium nitroprusside titrated to mean arterial pressure
options.explanation: Nitroprusside causes potent venodilation and arterial dilation, which exacerbates preload loss and worsens profound shock in RVI.

options.text: Sublingual administration of repeated doses of nitroglycerin until chest pain resolves
options.explanation: Nitroglycerin triggered this patient's hemodynamic collapse by reducing RV preload; additional doses will precipitate fatal cardiac arrest.

options.text: Intravenous bolus of metoprolol tartrate to reduce myocardial oxygen consumption
options.explanation: Beta-blockers abolish compensatory tachycardia and reduce inotropy, worsening cardiogenic shock in acute right ventricular infarction.

stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks gestation presents to the labor and delivery unit with progressive orthopnea, nocturnal cough, and severe lower extremity swelling for 1 week. She cannot lie flat without experiencing severe air hunger. Vital signs: blood pressure 138/88 mm Hg, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Physical examination reveals elevated JVP to 10 cm H2O, bibasilar crackles extending midway up both lung fields, an S3 gallop, and 3+ pitting edema to the mid-calves. 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia with non-specific ST-T changes. Transthoracic echocardiogram reveals global left ventricular hypokinesis, left ventricular end-diastolic dimension of 5.8 cm, and LVEF of 28%, with trace mitral regurgitation and absence of prior structural heart disease. Fetal heart rate monitoring is reassuring. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for this patient?

options.text: Immediate initiation of oral enalapril and spironolactone prior to delivery
options.explanation: ACE inhibitors (enalapril) and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone) are teratogenic/fetotoxic (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia) and contraindicated in pregnancy.

options.text: Urgent stabilized delivery planning with intravenous loop diuresis and therapeutic anticoagulation
options.explanation: This patient presents with PERIPARTUM CARDIOMYOPATHY (PPCM), defined as heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF <45%) developing toward the end of pregnancy (last month) or in the months following delivery (up to 5 months postpartum), in the absence of an identifiable pre-existing cardiac etiology. Risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, preeclampsia, and multiple gestation. Management of acute decompensated PPCM antepartum requires: (1) Aggressive heart failure stabilization with intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide) and vasodilators (hydralazine/nitrates; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and ARNIs are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy due to fetotoxicity); (2) THERAPEUTIC ANTICOAGULATION (with low-molecular-weight heparin): PPCM carries an exceptionally high risk of thromboembolism (>15-20%) driven by the combined hypercoagulability of pregnancy and low flow/stasis in dilated cardiac chambers (especially when LVEF <= 30%); and (3) URGENT DELIVERY PLANNING once the mother is hemodynamically stabilized. Vaginal delivery with epidural anesthesia is preferred unless there is hemodynamic instability or obstetrical indications for cesarean. Bromocriptine (inhibiting prolactin cleavage into cardiotoxic 16-kDa prolactin) may be considered as adjunctive therapy.

options.text: Elective termination of pregnancy deferred until 6 weeks postpartum after recovery of LVEF
options.explanation: The patient is at 37 weeks gestation (full term) in acute heart failure; delaying delivery until 6 weeks postpartum is inappropriate and dangerous.

options.text: Initiation of high-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate to prevent impending eclamptic seizures
options.explanation: Magnesium sulfate treats preeclampsia/eclampsia; in acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema, magnesium can depress myocardial function and worsen respiratory failure.

options.text: Complete bed rest with fluid boluses to maintain uterine and placental perfusion
options.explanation: Fluid boluses in acute heart failure with an LVEF of 28% and pulmonary edema will precipitate fatal respiratory failure and flash pulmonary edema.

topic: Ascending Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Surgical Repair Diameter Threshold
stem: A 46-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents for routine annual cardiovascular follow-up. He is asymptomatic and exercises regularly by walking. Physical examination reveals a tall, slender habitus, pectus excavatum, arachnodactyly, and arm span exceeding height. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, heart rate 64/min. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal heart sounds without murmurs. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates an ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm with a maximal root diameter of 5.1 cm; trileaflet aortic valve with trace regurgitation, and LVEF 60%. Repeat gated contrast-enhanced CT angiography confirms maximal aortic root diameter of 5.1 cm with normal descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. His family history is notable for an older brother with Marfan syndrome who suffered an acute aortic dissection at age 44. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.text: Conservative surveillance with repeat CT angiography in 12 months
options.explanation: Waiting 12 months in a Marfan patient with a 5.1 cm aorta and a family history of fatal dissection exceeds safe thresholds and risks fatal rupture.

options.text: Immediate initiation of high-dose oral aspirin and clopidogrel therapy
options.explanation: Antiplatelet therapy does not prevent aortic aneurysm expansion and increases bleeding risks if dissection occurs.

options.text: Elective surgical aortic root and ascending aortic replacement
options.explanation: This patient has an ASCENDING THORACIC AORTIC ANEURYSM (TAA) in the setting of MARFAN SYNDROME (fibrillin-1 gene mutation). The 2022 ACC/AHA and 2024 ESC guidelines establish clear DIAMETER THRESHOLDS FOR ELECTIVE SURGICAL REPAIR of thoracic aortic aneurysms: (1) In general, asymptomatic patients without genetic aortopathies: surgery is recommended when ascending aortic diameter reaches >= 5.5 cm; (2) In patients with MARFAN SYNDROME: the surgical threshold is lower, at >= 5.0 cm (or >= 4.5 cm if there are high-risk features such as family history of early dissection, rapid growth >0.3 cm/year, severe aortic regurgitation, or desire for pregnancy); (3) In Loeys-Dietz syndrome, threshold is even lower (>= 4.5 cm). Because this patient with Marfan syndrome has an aortic root measuring 5.1 cm AND a family history of premature aortic dissection in a first-degree relative, ELECTIVE SURGICAL REPAIR (valve-sparing aortic root replacement [David procedure] or composite valve-graft [Bentall procedure]) is strongly indicated to prevent catastrophic Type A dissection or rupture.

options.text: Endovascular stent-graft repair (TEVAR) of the ascending aortic root
options.explanation: TEVAR is technically contraindicated in the ascending aorta and root in genetic connective tissue disorders due to poor landing zones and extreme risk of retrograde Type A dissection.

options.text: Discontinuation of all antihypertensive medications to avoid hypotension
options.explanation: Strict blood pressure control (primarily with beta-blockers and ARBs) is essential to reduce aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt), not discontinuation.

topic: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome Endovascular Stenting vs Radiation Therapy
stem: A 61-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history presents with progressive facial swelling, neck fullness, and dyspnea that worsen when he bends over to tie his shoes or lies flat. Over the past 3 days, his voice has become hoarse, and he has developed mild stridor when agitated. Physical examination reveals marked plethora and non-pitting edema of the face, neck, and upper chest, with prominent collateral venous engorgement over the anterior thoracic wall. Raising both arms above his head for 1 minute produces intense facial congestion, cyanosis, and dizziness (positive Pemberton sign). Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrates a 6.5-cm right upper lobe mass compressing and invading the superior vena cava, with near-total luminal obstruction, extensive mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and mild extrinsic compression of the mid-trachea. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention to rapidly relieve life-threatening venous obstruction in this patient?

options.text: Immediate intravenous bolus of furosemide 80 mg followed by fluid restriction
options.explanation: Diuretics can decrease intravascular volume and precipitate thrombosis within the sluggish, obstructed SVC without relieving the extrinsic tumor compression.

options.text: Emergency open surgical resection of the superior vena cava with prosthetic Dacron graft bypass
options.explanation: Open surgical reconstruction carries high perioperative morbidity and mortality; endovascular stenting is the preferred, safe, minimally invasive standard of care.

options.text: Urgent whole-brain radiation therapy to prevent cerebral herniation
options.explanation: Radiation treats the brain, but does not relieve the thoracic obstruction causing venous hypertension; endovascular stenting is indicated.

options.text: Emergent endovascular superior vena cava angioplasty and stenting
options.explanation: This patient presents with severe SUPERIOR VENA CAVA (SVC) SYNDROME complicated by airway compromise (stridor, tracheal narrowing). SVC syndrome results from obstruction of blood flow through the SVC, most commonly caused by MALIGNANCY (~70-80% of cases, primarily non-small cell lung cancer, small cell lung cancer, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma). Characteristic manifestations include facial and neck edema, plethora, dilated collateral veins across the upper torso, and Pemberton sign (congestion on arm elevation). When acute airway compromise, stridor, or severe cerebral edema (headache, confusion, coma) is present, SVC syndrome is a life-threatening medical emergency. The treatment of choice for RAPID, IMMEDIATE RELIEF of obstruction is ENDOVASCULAR CAVAL RECANALIZATION WITH PERCUTANEOUS STENTING. Endovascular stenting provides symptom relief within 24 to 48 hours in >95% of patients, far more rapidly than radiation or chemotherapy, and does not interfere with subsequent histological biopsy or oncological therapy.

options.text: Empiric initiation of high-dose systemic thrombolytic therapy with alteplase
options.explanation: Systemic thrombolysis is indicated for acute catheter-associated thrombosis without malignancy; in neoplastic SVC compression, it risks fatal tumor hemorrhage without relieving mechanical mass effect.

topic: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Ultrasound Screening and Surgical Repair Indications
stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the clinic for a routine wellness examination. He has a 35-pack-year history of cigarette smoking, having quit 2 years ago, and hypertension managed with lisinopril. He is asymptomatic and denies back, flank, or abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 128/78 mm Hg and heart rate of 70/min. Abdominal palpation reveals a prominent, non-tender, pulsatile mass in the epigastrium and periumbilical region. A screening abdominal duplex ultrasound is performed, which reveals a fusiform infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) measuring 5.8 cm in maximal transverse diameter, with intraluminal thrombus. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.text: Repeat surveillance abdominal ultrasound in 6 months to assess expansion rate
options.explanation: Surveillance at 6 months is indicated for aneurysms 4.5 to 5.4 cm; at 5.8 cm, the aneurysm has crossed the 5.5-cm threshold and requires elective surgical repair.

options.text: Immediate therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban to dissolve intraluminal thrombus
options.explanation: Anticoagulation does not treat aneurysms and markedly increases mortality if the aneurysm ruptures; intraluminal thrombus is a normal feature of AAA.

options.text: Administration of oral propranolol titrated to target resting heart rate <50 beats/min
options.explanation: While beta-blockers treat thoracic aortic dissection, trials have shown they do not reduce AAA expansion rates or replace surgical repair.

options.text: Outpatient magnetic resonance elastography to measure wall shear stiffness
options.explanation: Elastography is an experimental research tool; clinical practice guidelines use maximum transverse diameter on ultrasound/CT to guide surgical repair.

options.text: Elective repair via endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) or open surgical graft replacement

topic: Statin-Associated Muscle Symptoms Creatine Kinase Re-challenge Strategy
stem: A 58-year-old man with coronary artery disease and prior stent placement 4 months ago presents with dull, aching pain and stiffness in his bilateral thighs and upper arms for 3 weeks. He denies dark urine, fever, or rash. Four months ago, he was initiated on atorvastatin 80 mg daily. Physical examination reveals normal muscle strength (5/5) in all extremities without muscle tenderness or fasciculations. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: serum creatine kinase (CK) 380 U/L (reference 30-200 U/L), serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and normal AST and ALT. Urinalysis is negative for blood and myoglobin. Atorvastatin is temporarily discontinued, and within 3 weeks, his muscle aches completely resolve and repeat serum CK normalizes to 110 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in lipid-lowering management?

options.text: Re-challenging with a lower dose of a different statin or intermittent dosing with rosuvastatin
options.explanation: This patient experienced STATIN-ASSOCIATED MUSCLE SYMPTOMS (SAMS, statin-induced myalgia/myopathy), the most common adverse effect of statin therapy. Management of mild-to-moderate SAMS without severe rhabdomyolysis (defined as CK <4-5 times upper limit of normal, here 380 U/L, normal renal function, no myoglobinuria) follows a structured algorithm: (1) Temporarily DISCONTINUE statin therapy until symptoms resolve and CK normalizes (typically 2-4 weeks); (2) RE-CHALLENGE with either: a LOWER DOSE of the same statin, a DIFFERENT STATIN with different pharmacokinetic properties (e.g., switching from lipophilic atorvastatin/simvastatin to hydrophilic pravastatin or rosuvastatin), or INTERMITTENT DOSING with a long half-life statin (e.g., rosuvastatin 5-10 mg twice weekly); and (3) If statin intolerance persists despite trials of at least two to three different statins, non-statin lipid-lowering agents (EZETIMIBE, PCSK9 inhibitors [evolocumab, alirocumab], or bempedoic acid) should be added to achieve guideline LDL-C targets. Completely abandoning statin therapy after a single episode of myalgia without re-challenge deprives high-risk coronary patients of proven secondary prevention cardiovascular mortality benefits.

options.text: Permanent cessation of all HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and initiation of gemfibrozil monotherapy
options.explanation: Gemfibrozil combined with or replacing statins impairs glucuronidation and has poor cardiovascular outcome data compared to statins; re-challenging statins is essential.

options.text: Immediate initiation of oral coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) supplementation while resuming atorvastatin 80 mg
options.explanation: Randomized controlled trials have consistently demonstrated that coenzyme Q10 does not prevent or improve statin-induced myopathy compared to placebo.

options.text: Performance of electromyography and quadriceps muscle biopsy before restarting therapy
options.explanation: Invasive EMG and muscle biopsy are indicated only for suspected immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (anti-HMGCR antibodies, CK >10-50x ULN), not mild SAMS.

options.text: Discharge with lifestyle modifications alone without pharmacotherapy, targeting LDL <160 mg/dL
options.explanation: Patients with established coronary artery disease require intensive LDL-C lowering (<70 mg/dL or <55 mg/dL) for secondary prevention; lifestyle alone is insufficient.

stem: A 64-year-old man with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy presents for routine outpatient follow-up. He reports mild dyspnea when climbing more than two flights of stairs (NYHA Class II), but denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or peripheral edema. His current medications are sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. Vital signs: blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, heart rate 64/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination is unremarkable, with clear lungs, normal JVP, and no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show: serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, potassium 4.6 mEq/L, and HbA1c 5.6%. Transthoracic echocardiogram reveals LVEF 32% with global hypokinesis. Which of the following pharmacotherapies should be added to this patient's regimen to provide additional reduction in all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization?

options.text: Oral digoxin 0.125 mg daily to improve myocardial inotropic performance
options.explanation: Digoxin reduces heart failure hospitalizations in symptomatic patients, but does NOT reduce all-cause or cardiovascular mortality in HFrEF.

options.text: An SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin 10 mg daily
options.explanation: Current international guidelines (ACC/AHA/HFSA and ESC) define the 'FOUR PILLARS' of Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT) for patients with HEART FAILURE WITH REDUCED EJECTION FRACTION (HFrEF, LVEF <= 40%): (1) ANGIOTENSIN RECEPTOR-NEPRILYSIN INHIBITOR (ARNI, sacubitril-valsartan) or ACEi/ARB; (2) EVIDENCE-BASED BETA-BLOCKER (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, or bisoprolol); (3) MINERALOCORTICOID RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST (MRA, spironolactone or eplerenone); and (4) SODIUM-GLUCOSE COTRANSPORTER-2 (SGLT2) INHIBITOR (EMPAGLIFLOZIN or DAPAGLIFLOZIN). Landmark randomized trials (DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced) demonstrated that adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to foundational GDMT reduces cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalizations by ~25%, improves quality of life, and slows renal function decline, REGARDLESS OF THE PRESENCE OR ABSENCE OF TYPE 2 DIABETES. SGLT2 inhibitors provide these benefits through osmotic diuresis, reduction in preload/afterload, enhanced myocardial energetics, and reduction in intraglomerular hypertension. The four pillars should be initiated and uptitrated promptly in all eligible HFrEF patients.

options.explanation: Hydralazine-isosorbide dinitrate provides mortality reduction specifically when added to GDMT in self-identified Black patients with persistent NYHA III-IV symptoms, or those intolerant to ARNI/ACEi.

options.text: Ivabradine 5 mg twice daily to lower resting heart rate
options.explanation: Ivabradine is indicated only for patients with sinus rhythm, resting heart rate >= 70 bpm despite maximally tolerated beta-blockade; this patient's HR is already 64 bpm.

options.text: High-dose loop diuretic with bumetanide 2 mg daily for decongestion
options.explanation: Loop diuretics relieve congestive symptoms, but have never been shown to reduce mortality; this patient is euvolemic and does not require increased diuresis.

subject: Medicine
topic: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy Apical Ballooning Supportive Care and Recovery
stem: A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with acute retrosternal chest pain and shortness of breath that began 2 hours after learning of her husband's sudden death in an automobile accident. She has no chronic medical conditions. Vital signs: blood pressure 104/68 mm Hg, heart rate 94/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Cardiovascular examination reveals an S3 gallop and soft bibasilar crackles without murmurs. 12-lead ECG demonstrates ST-segment elevations of 2 mm in leads V2-V5 with deep T-wave inversions. Serum troponin I is mildly elevated at 1.8 ng/mL (reference <0.04 ng/mL). She is taken emergently to the cardiac catheterization laboratory for suspected anterior STEMI. Coronary angiography reveals completely normal, widely patent epicardial coronary arteries without obstructive lesions, thrombosis, or dissection. Left ventriculography during systole reveals hyperkinesis of the basal left ventricular segments with profound akinesis and extensive ballooning of the mid-to-apical left ventricular walls (apical ballooning), resulting in an estimated LVEF of 30%. Which of the following is the most accurate prognosis and management principle for this condition?

options.text: Immediate placement of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for irreversible myocardial scar
options.explanation: Myocardial dysfunction in Takotsubo is transient metabolic stunning, not permanent scar tissue; ICDs are not indicated as LVEF spontaneously normalizes.

options.text: Emergency surgical placement of a durable left ventricular assist device
options.explanation: Durable LVADs are reserved for end-stage refractory heart failure, not a transient, reversible cardiomyopathy with rapid recovery.

options.text: Conservative supportive care with expected spontaneous recovery of left ventricular function within several weeks
options.explanation: This patient has STRESS-INDUCED (TAKOTSUBO) CARDIOMYOPATHY (also known as apical ballooning syndrome or 'broken heart syndrome'). It predominantly affects postmenopausal women and is typically triggered by intense emotional or physical stress (e.g., bereavement, surgery, catastrophic news). Pathogenesis involves a massive surge in circulating catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine), which causes microvascular coronary spasm, direct catecholamine myocardial toxicity (contraction band necrosis), and metabolic stunning. Clinical presentation mimics acute anterior STEMI: ischemic chest pain, ST-segment elevations in precordial leads, and elevated troponins (often modestly elevated, disproportionately low relative to the extensive territory of wall motion abnormality). Coronary angiography reveals NO OBSTRUCTIVE CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE. Left ventriculography characteristically demonstrates APICAL BALLOONING: severe akinesis of the apical and mid-ventricular segments with compensatory basal hyperkinesis, resembling a traditional Japanese octopus trap ('tako-tsubo'). Management is primarily SUPPORTIVE (treating transient heart failure with diuretics/afterload reduction). In the absence of early complications (cardiogenic shock, LVOT obstruction, apical thrombus), PROGNOSIS IS EXCELLENT, with >90-95% of patients demonstrating COMPLETE SPONTANEOUS RECOVERY of left ventricular systolic function within 4 to 8 weeks.

options.text: Lifelong therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin targeting INR 2.5 to 3.5
options.explanation: Anticoagulation is indicated only temporarily if an apical mural thrombus forms, and can be stopped once ventricular wall motion fully recovers.

options.text: Immediate initiation of high-dose inotropic therapy with epinephrine infusion
options.explanation: Exogenous catecholamines (epinephrine, dobutamine) worsen the underlying catecholamine-mediated myocardial toxicity and can trigger lethal LVOT obstruction.

topic: Post-Cardiac Arrest Targeted Temperature Management Normothermia Protocol
stem: A 54-year-old man collapses while jogging in a public park. Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is initiated immediately. Emergency medical services arrive 6 minutes later, document ventricular fibrillation, and achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after 1 defibrillation shock and 4 minutes of advanced cardiovascular life support. On arrival at the emergency department, he remains deeply comatose, opening his eyes only to noxious stimulation without purposeful motor response. Vital signs: blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg, heart rate 84/min, core body temperature 37.8 C (100.0 F), and oxygen saturation 98% on mechanical ventilation. 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation. Emergent coronary angiography reveals non-obstructive coronary disease. Which of the following represents the most appropriate neuroprotective strategy for this patient in the intensive care unit?

options.text: Rapid deep hypothermic cooling to a target core temperature of 28 C to 30 C
options.explanation: Deep hypothermia (<32 C) causes intractable ventricular arrhythmias, profound coagulopathy, severe immunosuppression, and increased mortality.

options.text: Administration of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone to suppress neuroinflammation
options.explanation: High-dose corticosteroids have not been shown to improve neurological outcomes in post-anoxic brain injury and increase secondary infection rates.

options.text: Performance of early neuroprognostication and withdrawal of life support within 24 hours
options.explanation: Neurological prognostication in comatose post-cardiac arrest patients must NEVER be performed prior to 72 hours after ROSC (and after normothermia re-establishment).

options.text: Targeted temperature management maintaining strict normothermia (36.0 C to 37.5 C) with active fever prevention
options.explanation: This patient is comatose following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with successful return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Post-cardiac arrest syndrome is characterized by post-anoxic brain injury, myocardial dysfunction, and systemic ischemia-reperfusion response. Following the landmark TTM-2 randomized trial and updated 2021-2023 international resuscitation guidelines (AHA and ERC/ESICM), TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT (TTM) is recommended for ALL comatose adult patients with ROSC after cardiac arrest. Current guidelines support TARGETING STRICT NORMOTHERMIA (36.0 C to 37.5 C) WITH ACTIVE PREVENTION AND TREATMENT OF FEVER (temperature >= 37.8 C) for at least 72 hours, or maintaining a controlled target temperature between 32 C and 36 C for at least 24 hours followed by controlled rewarming. High-quality evidence has shown that actively avoiding fever is as neuroprotective as hypothermia (33 C) while avoiding the coagulopathy, electrolyte shifts, and shivering complications of deep hypothermia. Even brief spikes of fever (>= 37.8 C) exponentially increase cerebral metabolic demand and worsen secondary neuronal apoptosis.

options.text: Induced hyperthermia to 38.5 C to enhance cerebral microvascular vasodilation
options.explanation: Hyperthermia markedly increases cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen, accelerates free radical formation, and causes catastrophic secondary brain injury.

topic: Acute Mitral Regurgitation Papillary Muscle Flail Leaflet Emergent Repair
stem: A 59-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe shortness of breath that awoke her from sleep 1 hour ago. She has a history of mild mitral valve prolapse diagnosed 10 years ago. On arrival, she is sitting bolt upright, gasping for breath, and coughing up pink, frothy sputum. Vital signs: blood pressure 92/64 mm Hg, heart rate 124/min, respiratory rate 34/min, and oxygen saturation 82% on 100% non-rebreather mask. Physical examination reveals cool extremities, elevated JVP, and diffuse bilateral coarse crackles and wheezes throughout both lung fields. Cardiovascular examination reveals a hyperdynamic apical impulse and an early-to-mid systolic murmur heard at the cardiac apex that radiates to the left axilla and base of the heart; the murmur is soft and ends well before S2. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates left ventricular hyperkinesis with LVEF 70%, normal left atrial dimensions, and complete flail of the posterior mitral valve leaflet into the left atrium during systole, producing an eccentric, massive regurgitant jet with dense continuous-wave Doppler signal and pulmonary vein systolic flow reversal. Which of the following is the definitive intervention for this patient?

options.text: Elective outpatient transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) scheduled in 6 weeks
options.explanation: Acute severe MR with cardiogenic pulmonary edema and a flail leaflet is a surgical emergency; delaying intervention will result in fatal respiratory or circulatory arrest.

options.text: Long-term oral anticoagulation with warfarin to prevent left atrial appendage thrombosis
options.explanation: The left atrium is normal-sized and non-dilated; anticoagulation does not treat mechanical valve disruption and will complicate emergent surgery.

options.text: Immediate high-dose intravenous beta-blockade to reduce left ventricular contractility
options.explanation: Negative inotropic agents worsen cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema in acute MR; contractility must be maintained to sustain forward cardiac output.

options.text: Administration of oral digoxin and spironolactone to promote left ventricular remodeling
options.explanation: Oral medications for chronic heart failure remodeling have no role in acute mechanical chordal rupture and hemodynamic collapse.

options.text: Emergent surgical mitral valve repair or replacement
options.explanation: This patient has ACUTE SEVERE MITRAL REGURGITATION (MR) caused by acute rupture of the chordae tendineae complicating myxomatous MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE (MVP), resulting in a FLAIL POSTERIOR MITRAL LEAFLET. Unlike chronic MR, where the left atrium has years to dilate and accommodate regurgitant volume at low pressure, in ACUTE MR the normal-sized, non-compliant left atrium experiences a sudden, massive influx of systolic volume.
